sections.skill: Choose a measure that matches the goal of a task

questions.domain: Work: measuring how well AI works
questions.prompt: What should a measure match?
questions.intro: A MEASURE should match the GOAL of the task. If a tool flags rare problems, "percent correct" can mislead: if only 2 of 100 parcels are damaged, a tool that always says "fine" is 98% correct and catches nothing. Better measures look at what matters: how many damaged parcels were CAUGHT (out of all damaged ones), and how many flags were RIGHT (out of all flags). For a writing tool, the goal might be "fewer edits needed" or "readers understand it," not word count. Ask: "If this number improves, is the real goal closer?"

sections.skill: Compare measures with judging a basketball player

questions.domain: Work: measuring how well AI works
questions.prompt: What does judging only by points miss?
questions.intro: Judging a basketball player only by POINTS SCORED misses a lot: a defender who blocks shots and passes well helps the team win but may score little. And a player who takes 40 shots to score 20 points is not as helpful as the number suggests. The real goal is helping the team win, so coaches use several measures that connect to that goal. Measures for AI tools should connect to the real goal in the same way.

questions.domain: Work: measuring how well AI works
questions.prompt: A help desk is measured on "tickets closed," and staff close tickets without solving problems. What happened?

choices.text: The goal improved a lot, because closing more tickets always means more problems are solved
The number improved without the goal improving

questions.correct_answer: The number improved without the goal improving
questions.intro: When a measure becomes a target, people and systems can improve the number without improving the goal: a help desk measured on "tickets closed" may close tickets without solving problems. Use more than one measure, include one that reflects real outcomes (such as customers who did not need to contact you again), and look at examples behind the numbers.
